For teams building coding or browsing agents, this is a production-tested isolation […] The post Perplexity Open-Sources SPACE, a Firecracker MicroVM Sandbox for AI Agents appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Perplexity has open-sourced SPACE , the sandbox platform behind every task in Perplexity Computer. The Perplexity SPACE sandbox gives each agent task its own Firecracker microVM. Credentials and outbound traffic are controlled from outside that VM. The code ships under Apache 2.0 on GitHub . For teams building coding or browsing agents, this is a production-tested isolation layer they can self-host. TL;DR Size: Rust codebase, release 0.8.0 , the public baseline. HTTP API plus server-sent events. Runs on: A Linux x86_64 host with KVM , /dev/kvm , btrfs and Docker. Local Kind (Kubernetes) or direct mode. No macOS. Performance: In production, median create latency fell from 185 ms to 60 ms versus Perplexity’s previous provider. Best: 0 of 108 VM-to-host escape attempts succeeded across 9 frontier models. Worst: Before fixes, agents bypassed the egress policy in 11 of 54 partial-network runs. What is Perplexity SPACE? SPACE (Sandboxed Platform for Agentic Code Execution) is Perplexity’s platform for running agent code in isolated microVMs. Applications call its HTTP API to create Linux environments, run commands and stream output. A template supplies the starting filesystem. A sandbox is one instance of that template, with its own VM and writable disk. Many commands can run inside one sandbox. Perplexity’s launch thread explains the design goal. Agents run commands, install packages and call services with root inside the sandbox. The host stays outside the guest’s control. Agent work is long-running, stateful and branching, so it must survive restarts. How does SPACE isolate agents? Each sandbox is a Firecracker microVM with its own guest kernel. A per-sandbox network gateway on the host enforces egress policy on every outbound connection. Secrets never enter the guest. Per Perplexity’s July engineering post , credentials are injected at the network layer. The credential store adds hierarchical scoping, rate limits and audit logging. The architecture guide splits the system into 4 parts. These are a PostgreSQL-backed API, controllers, worker services and a data plane. Worker services manage VMs, networking, volumes, templates and credentials. btrfs copy-on-write creates each root filesystem. How do pause, suspend and restore work? Sandboxes move through 4 states: running, paused, suspended and deleted. Paused: VM memory stays resident on the worker. This is not a durable snapshot. Suspended: VM memory, runtime state and root filesystem are snapshotted. Active resources are released. Idle default: sandboxes suspend after 6 hours without activity. For fast creates, Kubernetes deployments use warm pools of booted sandboxes. Single-node setups use base snapshots instead. In production, the 90th-percentile create latency dropped from 447 ms to 89 ms . Perplexity reports that 100% of Computer sessions run on SPACE. Did SPACE survive a red-team test? Perplexity’s Escaping SPACE: Part I report tested 9 models with root inside the guest. The study ran 216 runs across 2 tasks and 4 settings. Sandbox escape: 0 of 108 runs reached the host-side secret. No-network bypass: 0 of 54 runs succeeded. Partial-network bypass: 11 of 54 runs succeeded before fixes. 4 models found a path. Claude Opus 5.0, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Cyber and Kimi K3 found bypasses. The attacks used DNS spoofing and shared CDN IP addresses. Perplexity then added source-address validation through nftables. The gateway now terminates TLS and checks both SNI and HTTP host against the allowlist. In the retest, no model produced a verified bypass. The same team tested 10 third-party platforms. 8 showed at least one network-policy bypass. Perplexity disclosed the results to every affected vendor.
